# Psychosocial {#sec-psychosocial}

Psychosocial data help researchers understand the complex relationship between psychological, emotional, behavioral, and social aspects of life and their influence on health outcomes. The Acute to Chronic Pain Signatures Study (A2CPS) includes several psychosocial assessments and associated Helping End Addiction Long-term (HEAL) Common Data Elements\ [@wandner_nih_2022] to gain a comprehensive understanding of chronic pain\ [@berardi_multi_2022]. For a general introduction to psychosocial assessments in clinical research, see resources such as the [NIH HEAL Initiative Common Data Elements](https://heal.nih.gov/data/common-data-elements).

This kit focuses on the two mood-disorder measures: depression, measured with the 8-item Patient Health Questionnaire-8 (PHQ-8)\ [@kroenke_phq_2009], and anxiety, measured with the 7-item Generalized Anxiety Disorder scale (GAD-7)\ [@spitzer_brief_2006].

The files are pulled from the NIMH Data Archive (NDA) named `phq9`, but the study used the 8-item PHQ-8. Item 9 (thoughts of self-harm) was dropped from the study forms; the `phq9_9` column is a carry-over from NDA's data structure, coded `-9` for everyone, so we leave it out of scoring.

## Starting Project

### Locate Data

The psychosocial measures arrive from NDA as separate files, one per instrument, using NDA's own short field names. After downloading the psychosocial structures from your NDA data package, place them under `NDA_data/` so the project looks like this:

```bash
NDA_data/
└── Psychosocial/
    ├── gad7.csv
    └── phq9.csv
```

The code below reaches these files with `here()`, which resolves paths from the project root, so a chunk runs the same regardless of the working directory.

### Extract Data

Often, researchers want to examine the relationship between different psychosocial measures. For example, Anxiety (GAD-7) and Depression (PHQ-8) frequently coexist due to shared biological mechanisms.

To explore this, we first load the relevant datasets. As each file is read, we recode `record_id` to numeric data type and drop any exact duplicate rows so that a participant appears only once.

```{r}
#| label: setup

library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(here)
library(readr)

# in NDA files a -9 marks an item the participant left blank
blank_to_na <- \(x) na_if(x, -9)
```

```{r}
#| label: load-gad

gad <- read_csv(here("NDA_data", "Psychosocial", "gad7.csv"), skip = 1) |>
  rename(record_id = src_subject_id) |>
  mutate(record_id = as.numeric(record_id))

# guard: every record_id must parse to a number before filtering and cohort assignment
if (any(is.na(gad$record_id))) {
  stop(sum(is.na(gad$record_id)), " record_id value(s) did not parse to a number")
}

test_records <- c(10000, 15000, 20000, 25000, 40000, 50000,
                  60000, 70000, 80000, 90000, 100000, 110000, 120000)

gad <- gad |>
  distinct() |>
  filter(!record_id %in% test_records) |>
  mutate(cohort = case_when(
    record_id >= 10000 & record_id < 15000 | record_id >= 25000 ~ "TKA",
    .default = "Thoracic"
  ))
```

```{r}
#| label: load-phq

phq <- read_csv(here("NDA_data", "Psychosocial", "phq9.csv"), skip = 1) |>
  rename(record_id = src_subject_id) |>
  mutate(record_id = as.numeric(record_id))

# guard: every record_id must parse to a number before filtering and cohort assignment
if (any(is.na(phq$record_id))) {
  stop(sum(is.na(phq$record_id)), " record_id value(s) did not parse to a number")
}

phq <- phq |>
  distinct() |>
  filter(!record_id %in% test_records) |>
  mutate(cohort = case_when(
    record_id >= 10000 & record_id < 15000 | record_id >= 25000 ~ "TKA",
    .default = "Thoracic"
  ))
```

The downloaded files use the NDA's short field names (`gad7_1`, `gad7_2`, and so on). We first rename them to the HEAL Common Data Element names, which the NIH HEAL Initiative defined so that measures are recorded consistently and can be compared across HEAL studies. The mapping below comes from the A2CPS crosswalk. Note that `gad7_8` holds the survey language rather than a GAD item, so it is left out.

```{r}
#| label: rename-gad

gad_crosswalk <- c(
  GAD2FeelNervScl = "gad7_1",
  GAD2NotStopWryScl = "gad7_2",
  GAD7WryTooMchScl = "gad7_3",
  GAD7TroubRelxScl = "gad7_4",
  GAD7RstlessScl = "gad7_5",
  GAD7EasyAnnoyedScl = "gad7_6",
  GAD7FeelAfrdScl = "gad7_7"
)

gad <- gad |>
  rename(all_of(gad_crosswalk))
```

NDA provides the individual item responses rather than the summary scores, so we compute them here. A missing response is coded `-9`, so we convert those to `NA` before scoring. For GAD-7, when at least five of the seven items are answered we fill any missing items with that person's rounded item mean\ [@Arrieta2017] and then sum the seven items; with fewer than five answered items the score is left missing.

```{r}
#| label: score-gad

gad_items <- names(gad_crosswalk)

# GAD-7 is scored only when at least 5 of its 7 items are answered
gad_min_answered <- 5

gad <- gad |>
  # turn blank items into missing values
  mutate(across(all_of(gad_items), blank_to_na)) |>
  # count how many items each person actually answered
  mutate(gad_n_answered = rowSums(!is.na(across(all_of(gad_items))))) |>
  # fill a blank item with the person's own rounded average, then add the items up
  mutate(
    gad_item_mean = if_else(
      gad_n_answered >= gad_min_answered,
      round(rowMeans(across(all_of(gad_items)), na.rm = TRUE)),
      NA_real_
    ),
    across(all_of(gad_items), \(x) coalesce(x, gad_item_mean)),
    imputed_gad_score = if_else(
      gad_n_answered >= gad_min_answered,
      rowSums(across(all_of(gad_items))),
      NA_real_
    )
  ) |>
  select(-gad_item_mean)
```

PHQ follows the same pattern. We rename the eight PHQ-8 items to their HEAL names using the crosswalk. The ninth item (`phq9_9`) is excluded as described above, and `phq9_10` records the survey language rather than a response.

```{r}
#| label: rename-phq

phq_crosswalk <- c(
  PHQLitIntrstScore = "phq9_1",
  PHQDeprssnScore = "phq9_2",
  PHQSleepImpairScore = "phq9_3",
  PHQTirdLittleEnrgyScore = "phq9_4",
  PHQAbnrmlDietScore = "phq9_5",
  PHQFlngFailrScore = "phq9_6",
  PHQConcntrtnImprmntScore = "phq9_7",
  PHQMovmntSpchImprmntScore = "phq9_8"
)

phq <- phq |>
  rename(all_of(phq_crosswalk))
```

Missing responses are coded `-9` here as well, so we apply the same recode and then sum the eight items when at least seven of them are answered.

```{r}
#| label: score-phq

phq_items <- names(phq_crosswalk)

# PHQ-8 is scored only when at least 7 of its 8 items are answered
phq_min_answered <- 7

phq <- phq |>
  # turn blank items into missing values
  mutate(across(all_of(phq_items), blank_to_na)) |>
  # count how many items each person actually answered
  mutate(phq_n_answered = rowSums(!is.na(across(all_of(phq_items))))) |>
  # add the items up, leaving the score missing when too few were answered
  mutate(
    phq_score = if_else(
      phq_n_answered >= phq_min_answered,
      rowSums(across(all_of(phq_items)), na.rm = TRUE),
      NA_real_
    )
  )
```

Next, we join the two datasets. A few background columns can differ between forms, since a person may complete GAD and PHQ on different days or in different languages, so we first label `interview_age`, `interview_date`, and `language` with a `gad_` or `phq_` prefix. That leaves the stable identifiers as the only shared columns, so we join on all of them with `intersect()`. The identifier `record_id` links records across psychosocial forms and to other modalities (like neuroimaging or genomics), and `inner_join` keeps only rows present in both tables.

```{r}
#| label: join

# a few background columns can differ between forms, so label them by form first
form_cols <- c("interview_age", "interview_date", "language")
gad <- gad |> rename_with(\(x) paste0("gad_", x), all_of(form_cols))
phq <- phq |> rename_with(\(x) paste0("phq_", x), all_of(form_cols))

# the remaining shared columns are the stable identifiers, so join on all of them
gad_phq <- inner_join(gad, phq, by = intersect(names(gad), names(phq)))
```

View columns available after merging the two datasets

```{r}
#| label: peek

head(gad_phq)
```

Check data types and ensure that character variables are not stored as numeric, and that numeric variables are stored with the correct numeric type, not as character or factor.

```{r}
#| label: check-types

glimpse(gad_phq)
```

## Exploratory data analysis

Anxiety and depression frequently coexist due to shared biological mechanisms and overlapping symptoms. Approximately 50% of patients with depression also meet the criteria for having an anxiety disorder. The co-occurrence of anxiety and depression in an individual increases the risk of suicide, affects social interactions, and results in more hospitalizations\ [@kircanski_investigating_2017]. We are interested in looking at the association between Anxiety scores and Depression scores. While looking at the datatypes, spearman correlation would be the measure of choice since we have confirmed using the `glimpse()` function that those variables are stored as ordered and numeric.

**Spearman Correlation**:

Since GAD and PHQ scores are ordered but not continuous, spearman correlation here would be a better choice than pearson since it measures monotonic association between two variables by comparing their ranks, we will set `method = "spearman"` and add `use = "complete.obs"` to ignore rows with missing values.

```{r}
#| label: correlation

cor(
  gad_phq$imputed_gad_score,
  gad_phq$phq_score,
  method = "spearman",
  use = "complete.obs"
)
```

As expected we see a strong positive correlation between anxiety and depression within the A2CPS cohort, around 0.73. Let's visualize these results with a simple boxplot.

```{r}
#| label: gad-phq-boxplot

# Remove rows with NA in either column
gad_phq_clean <- gad_phq |>
  filter(!is.na(imputed_gad_score), !is.na(phq_score))

# Create the plot
ggplot(
  gad_phq_clean,
  aes(
    x = factor(imputed_gad_score),
    y = phq_score,
    fill = factor(imputed_gad_score)
  )
) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(
    title = "PHQ Score Distribution by GAD Score",
    x = "GAD Score (Imputed)",
    y = "PHQ Score",
    fill = "GAD Score"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  stat_summary(aes(group = 1), fun = median, geom = "line", linewidth = 1) 
```

We see that there is a positive association between Anxiety and Depression scores.

## Considerations While Working on the Project

### Data Generation

Self-reported psychosocial assessments were collected electronically from participants. A2CPS includes the core psychosocial assessments and associated HEAL Common Data Elements for harmonization, and remote assessments were implemented for both English and Spanish-speaking participants. Of note: two psychosocial items were also collected during brain-imaging sessions, a pain assessment and a mood assessment.

### Data Quality

Like all self-reported data, these assessments may contain errors or missing values, and the responses were cleaned and checked before being deposited in NDA. Each instrument is provided as its own file, and the cohort is recovered from `record_id` as shown above.

### Cross-Modality Links

Each file includes `record_id` along with NDA's `subjectkey`, which serve as unique identifiers and enable linkage across psychosocial data files as well as other data modalities.

### Missing Data

Proceed with caution when merging data across psychosocial data or different modalities. Merging datasets often leads to a reduced sample size due to missing data or incomplete forms. This can lower statistical power and limit the ability to draw reliable conclusions.
